facts.text: Rich Square’s name honors the town’s early prosperity; it was renamed in 1937 after William Spencer Creecy, a local historian and state treasurer.
The Duke-Lawrence House, a Georgian gem, sits in Rich Square and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.
Quaker settlers founded Rich Square’s first Friends congregation in 1760, making it a historic center for the Religious Society of Friends in North Carolina.
During the Civil War, Northampton County’s Rich Square defended the Wilmington and Weldon Railroad, a vital supply line for Confederate forces.
Rich Square’s Holoman‑Outland House, an example of Colonial Revival architecture, earned a spot on the National Register in 2001.
The town’s elevation is just 22 meters (72 feet) above sea level, placing it among North Carolina’s low‑lying communities.
